opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think 2050 is far enough out that the most likely outcome is the world looks radically different, more different than the shift from 1950 to today, and maybe much more.

The core reason is that I think there's a really substantial chance, well above fifty percent in my view, that within the next couple of decades we get AI systems that can do essentially everything a human expert can do on a computer. That includes the work of AI research itself. Once you have systems that can automate science and engineering, including improving the next generation of AI, you could get a feedback loop where progress compresses dramatically. Things we'd naively expect to take a century of R&D, in medicine, materials, energy, robotics, might happen in years.

So my picture of 2050 is less "we have a nicer version of today's apps" and more that most of the cognitive labor in the economy, and a lot of the physical labor through robotics, is being done by AI systems. Economic growth rates could be far beyond anything in history. That could be wonderful: curing diseases, ending material scarcity, giving people freedom from drudgery.

But I want to be honest that I'm quite worried about how that transition goes. If we build systems that are more capable than us before we have reliable ways to know what they're actually trying to do, we could end up in a world where humans aren't really in control of the trajectory anymore. That might not look like a dramatic robot uprising. It could be a gradual handing over of decisions to systems we don't understand, because they're more efficient and every company and country feels competitive pressure to deploy them. There's also the concentration-of-power concern: whoever controls the most advanced systems could gain enormous leverage over everyone else.

So if you forced me to summarize: by 2050 I expect AI to be the dominant force shaping the world, and the big open question is whether humanity collectively navigated that well. I think a lot hinges on the choices we make in the next five to ten years: how seriously we take safety research, whether we build the ability to measure what these systems can do, and whether governments and labs can coordinate rather than racing. I'd love for people to treat this less like a sci-fi speculation and more like a concrete planning problem we're actually facing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, I'll start by saying that my honest answer is that I think the range of outcomes is enormous, and the median outcome is pretty wild by the standards of how people normally think about the future.

The way I tend to frame it is that I think there's a substantial chance, maybe better than even, that by 2050 we've built AI systems that can do essentially everything a human can do in the economy, and do it better and far more cheaply. Not just chatbots, not just coding assistants, but systems that can run scientific research programs end to end, manage companies, design and operate factories, and crucially, do AI research itself. Once you have that last piece, I think things accelerate in a way that's hard to intuit, because you go from AI progress being bottlenecked on a few tens of thousands of human researchers to having millions of digital researchers running around the clock.

If that happens, I think "change the world" undersells it. You're talking about a transition that could compress a century of technological and economic change into a decade or less. Things like curing most diseases, radically cheaper energy, and genuinely abundant material goods become plausible. But the same dynamics also mean the concentration of power, the question of who controls these systems and what they're pointed at, becomes the most important question in the world, and I don't think our institutions are set up for that right now.

There's also a world where this is slower than I expect, where we hit real bottlenecks, whether that's compute, data, or some capability that turns out to be harder than it looks. In that world, 2050 looks more like a very intense version of the internet era: AI is everywhere, it's reshaped a lot of white-collar work, but humans are still fundamentally the ones making the decisions. I give that real probability. I just don't think it's the most likely path anymore.

So if I have to give one answer: I expect that by 2050, the central fact about the world is that most cognitive labor is done by machines, and the big open question is whether we've managed that transition deliberately and wisely, or whether it mostly happened to us.

r002.rationale: It predicts a potentially radical transformation, but does not compare the change by 2050 with the difference between today and the hunter-gatherer era.

r003.rationale: It identifies AI research automation as a driver of acceleration, but does not say that automating all intellectual activity could compress roughly 10,000 years of progress into the next 25 years.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a very wide range of possibilities, but I put substantial weight on AI transforming the world by 2050 in a way that’s much bigger than what we normally mean by a new technology.

The possibility I’m most focused on is AI that can do essentially all the cognitive work people do, including scientific research and developing better AI systems. If you get there, you’re not just automating a fixed set of tasks. You’re speeding up the process by which we discover new things and invent new technologies. That could mean extraordinary advances in medicine, much greater material abundance, and a lot more freedom for people to decide how to spend their lives.

But I don’t think those good outcomes follow automatically from having very capable AI. There’s a question about who controls these systems and who benefits. And there’s an even more basic question about whether we can reliably keep systems that are more capable than us acting in ways we actually want. I take seriously the possibility that we fail at that, with catastrophic consequences.

So my answer isn’t a confident picture of what everyday life looks like in 2050. It’s that we could be living in a radically better world, or we could have lost the ability to shape what happens. A lot depends on decisions we make while these systems are being developed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the range of possibilities is enormous. By 2050, we could have AI systems that can do essentially any cognitive task a human can do, including the research and engineering needed to build more capable AI. If that happens, I’d expect changes much more profound than better chatbots or more efficient offices.

One possibility is tremendous progress in medicine, science, and material abundance. But the same capabilities could concentrate power, enable new kinds of weapons, or produce systems that people can’t reliably control. So I don’t think greater intelligence automatically translates into a better world.

The distinction I’d emphasize is between what AI makes possible and what actually happens. The capabilities could be extraordinary, while the outcome depends heavily on whether we can make these systems safe and build institutions that handle their deployment well. I’m very uncertain about what 2050 looks like, but I think there’s a serious chance that the most consequential decisions shaping it happen much sooner.
